title: An ordinary evening
hook: Seneca waits for the lamp to go out, then puts his own day on trial
tomorrow: what did the Prophet give his daughter instead of what she asked?

segments.voice: Yunmen answered his own question: every day is a good day, because it's the one you're in. Then evening comes, and so does the replay.

Lights off, phone face down, and the replay starts: the thing you said in the meeting, the text you sent too fast. A Roman named Seneca had a stranger habit, and he tells us exactly when he did it. Every night, once the lamp had been carried out of the room, and once his wife, who knew his habit, had gone quiet, he started on purpose. So why wait for the dark and the silence? What was he doing in there?
screen: `LIGHTS OFF. THE REPLAY STARTS.` → `SENECA WAITS FOR THE LAMP TO GO.` → `WHAT WAS HE DOING?`

segments.voice: He was putting his day on trial. Seneca was a Stoic philosopher, and he describes this in his book On Anger. He took the habit from an older teacher, Sextius, who asked himself at the end of each day: what bad habit have you cured today? What fault have you resisted? In what are you better? So Seneca pleads his own case every evening. He goes over the whole day, his words and his deeds, and hides nothing from himself. Then the surprise: the judge is kind. He even gives a sample verdict. In that argument you spoke too sharply; next time, don't take on people who won't learn. See that you don't do it again; this time I forgive you. That's the Stoic evening review as Seneca kept it: an honest look, one correction, a pardon, then sleep. Seneca says the sleep that follows is calm and deep. Now set that beside the midnight replay. The replay is a court with only a prosecutor, and the case never closes. Seneca's court has a judge, and it ends with a sentence that lets you go to bed. Perhaps that's why he waited for the dark: the day was done. The evening's job was to hear it once, fairly, and close the case.
screen: `SENECA PUTS HIS DAY ON TRIAL.` · `SEXTIUS'S THREE QUESTIONS.` · `HIDE NOTHING. THEN FORGIVE.` · `A JUDGE, NOT JUST A PROSECUTOR.` · then, large: `THE EVENING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and walk back through today, words and deeds, the way Seneca did. Stop at one moment you'd do differently, and give it a fair verdict in one sentence: next time, I'll do this instead. Then pardon it, and let the rest of the sit be quiet.
An ordinary evening: for Seneca, not leftover time, but the hour when the day gets one honest hearing and then closes.
Your line: the evening is the day's fair hearing. Seneca's verdict ended in a pardon. Sleep well.
